content: A lesion originates from the Latin term laesio, which translates to injury. It refers to any abnormal tissue present within or on an organism, typically resulting from disease or trauma. Lesions can arise from any process that causes tissue damage. For instance, a cancerous tumor itself is considered a lesion, but the surrounding tissue that becomes damaged due to the tumor is also classified as a lesion. Traumatic events, such as electrocution or chemical burns, can lead to the formation of lesions. Certain diseases are characterized by the presence of lesions, such as the skin abnormalities seen in chickenpox. Metabolic processes can also result in lesions, such as ulcers, or autoimmune activity, as observed in various forms of arthritis. In some cases, lesions are deliberately created during medical procedures, such as neurosurgery, where carefully placed brain lesions are used to treat conditions like epilepsy or other neurological disorders. It is important to note that lesions are not exclusive to humans or animals; plants can also develop lesions when they sustain damage. Given the broad definition of lesions, their types and classifications are nearly limitless. Lesions are categorized based on their specific characteristics. For example, lesions caused by cancer are classified as either malignant or benign. They may also be described by their shape, such as the bullseye or target appearance seen in certain ulcers. The size of a lesion can be classified as either gross (visible to the naked eye) or histologic (requiring a microscope for visualization). Another classification system distinguishes between space-occupying and non-space-occupying lesions. A space-occupying lesion, as the term implies, takes up physical space and may compress nearby structures, whereas a non-space-occupying lesion represents a void in the tissue, such as a region of the brain that has liquefied following a stroke. Some lesions are given specific names based on their unique characteristics or associations. For example, Ghon lesions are found in the lungs of individuals with tuberculosis. The distinctive skin lesions caused by the varicella-zoster virus are referred to as chickenpox. Lesions affecting the teeth are commonly known as dental caries. Lesions are also frequently classified by their anatomical location, such as skin lesions versus brain lesions.
